Option A, truth-in-advertising, concerns the accuracy of promotional claims, not steering a customer toward an unsuitable option. Option B, antitrust rules, governs agreements between competing businesses, not an individual sales interaction. Option D, copyright rules, protects creative works and has nothing to do with this selling practice.

question: A banquet team lead wants a single chart plotting each task's start date and duration against a calendar before a large event. Which tool should the team lead use?

options.A: A Gantt chart of task dates and durations
options.B: A PERT network diagram
options.C: A critical path diagram
options.D: A basic checklist listing tasks with no dates

explanation: A Gantt chart plots each task against a calendar with start dates and durations, which is exactly what the team lead needs. A PERT diagram and a critical path diagram emphasize task dependencies rather than calendar placement, and a basic checklist without dates cannot show duration or overlap at all.

question: A conference coordinator wants to know which sequence of tasks, if delayed, would push back the entire event's start time. Which tool identifies that sequence?

options.A: A Gantt chart of all tasks
options.B: A checklist ranked by personal preference
options.C: A critical path diagram
options.D: A PERT network diagram

explanation: A critical path diagram identifies the sequence of dependent tasks with no slack time, so a delay anywhere on it delays the whole event. A Gantt chart displays a timeline but not which sequence is critical, a PERT diagram maps dependencies without highlighting the critical sequence, and a personal-preference checklist reflects no schedule logic at all.

question: Three weeks before a hotel's annual gala, the event planner discovers two vendor deliveries are scheduled for the same day the ballroom must be reset, risking a conflict. Which project-management step best prevents the clash?

options.A: Cross-check the schedule and move one delivery
options.B: Wait until the week of the gala to see if the vendors coordinate on their own
options.C: Cancel one vendor's delivery entirely without notice
options.D: Add a third vendor to help manage the reset

explanation: Cross-checking the master schedule catches the conflict early and lets the planner reassign one delivery before it collides with the ballroom reset, which is the core discipline of project scheduling. Waiting for the vendors to coordinate on their own leaves the conflict undetected since neither vendor sees the other's timeline. Cancelling a delivery without notice risks the vendor relationship and does not use the schedule to solve the problem. Adding a third vendor increases coordination complexity instead of resolving the existing conflict.

performanceIndicator: Calculate RevPAR from ADR and occupancy
question: Cedar Peak Lodge has an average daily rate of $120 and an occupancy rate of 60%. What is its RevPAR?

options.A: $180.00, the ADR plus the occupancy rate
options.B: $72.00 per available room
options.C: $120.00, treating the full ADR alone as the RevPAR
options.D: $45.00, half of the average daily rate

explanation: RevPAR equals ADR multiplied by the occupancy rate, so $120 x 0.60 gives $72.00 per available room. The other options either add the two figures together, treat the ADR alone as RevPAR while ignoring occupancy, or simply halve the ADR, none of which is the correct formula.

performanceIndicator: Calculate RevPAR from ADR and occupancy
question: The Marbury Suites reports an average daily rate of $150 and an occupancy rate of 68% for July. A manager wants to know the property's RevPAR for the month to compare against budget.

options.A: $150.00, since ADR already reflects full occupancy
options.B: $102.00 per available room, reflecting 68% occupancy applied to the rate
options.C: $218.00, the ADR plus the occupancy percentage as dollars
options.D: $51.00, half of the average daily rate

explanation: RevPAR is ADR multiplied by occupancy, so $150 x 0.68 equals $102.00 per available room, the correct comparison figure for July. Treating the ADR itself as RevPAR ignores that occupancy was well under 100%. Adding the occupancy percentage to the ADR as if it were a dollar figure mixes two different units and produces a meaningless total. Halving the ADR has no basis in the RevPAR formula at all.

performanceIndicator: Calculate as-purchased vs edible-portion quantity (yield percentage)
question: A kitchen buys 50 lb of salmon fillets as-purchased. After trimming, 40 lb of edible portion remains. What is the yield percentage?

options.A: 80% yield percentage
options.B: 20%, trim weight measured against the AP weight
options.C: 125% yield percentage
options.D: 90% yield percentage

explanation: Yield percentage equals edible portion divided by as-purchased weight, so 40 lb divided by 50 lb equals 80%. Measuring the trim weight against the AP weight instead gives the loss percentage, not the yield; inverting the fractions produces the impossible value of 125%; and 90% does not match either number in the stem.

performanceIndicator: Calculate as-purchased vs edible-portion quantity (yield percentage)
question: A restaurant's walk-in cooler shows 90 lb of whole chickens as-purchased. After butchering, the kitchen yields 63 lb of edible portion, and the chef wants the yield percentage to update the standard recipe cost card.

options.A: 128.6% yield on the recipe cost card
options.B: 30.0% yield for the whole chickens
options.C: 63.0% yield
options.D: 70.0% yield for the whole chickens on the recipe cost card

explanation: Yield percentage is edible portion divided by as-purchased weight, so 63 lb divided by 90 lb gives 70.0%, the figure that belongs on the recipe cost card. Option A reports a yield above 100%, which is impossible because the edible portion is always less than the as-purchased weight it came from. Option B expresses the trim loss of 27 lb as a share of the as-purchased weight, which is the loss rate and not the yield. Option C treats the edible-portion pounds directly as a percentage, ignoring the as-purchased weight entirely.

question: The Aspen Creek Hotel earns $9,000 in room revenue from 60 rooms sold in one night. What is its average daily rate (ADR)?

options.A: $60.00 average daily rate
options.B: $150.00 per room sold
options.C: $9,000.00, the total revenue undivided by rooms sold
options.D: $100.00 average daily rate

explanation: ADR equals total room revenue divided by rooms sold, so $9,000 divided by 60 rooms equals $150.00. Using the full $9,000 without dividing by rooms sold reports total revenue, not a per-room rate, and $60.00 and $100.00 do not match either number given in the stem.

question: The Foothill Inn sold 80 rooms last night. Three of those rooms were comped and generated no revenue, while the remaining rooms brought in $15,400 in total room revenue. What is the ADR based on the rooms that generated revenue?

options.A: $192.50, dividing the revenue by all 80 rooms sold
options.B: $200.00, dividing the revenue by the 77 paying rooms
options.C: $5,133.33, dividing the revenue by the three comped rooms
options.D: $15,400.00, the total room revenue reported without dividing by any room count

explanation: ADR is calculated only on rooms that generated revenue, so the $15,400 in revenue divided by the 77 paying rooms gives $200.00. Dividing by all 80 rooms sold understates the rate by including the three comped rooms that earned nothing. Dividing by just the three comped rooms confuses the excluded rooms with the denominator entirely. Reporting the total revenue itself is not a rate at all, since it was never divided by any room count.

question: A restaurant serves 120 covers on Saturday night and records $3,600 in total food and beverage sales. What is the average check per cover?

options.A: $30.00 average check
options.B: $3,600.00, the total sales undivided by covers
options.C: $120.00 average check
options.D: $3.60 average check

explanation: Average check equals total sales divided by covers served, so $3,600 divided by 120 covers equals $30.00. Reporting the $3,600 total without dividing by covers gives total sales, not an average; using the covers count itself as a dollar figure or dropping two decimal places both misapply the numbers in the stem.

question: The Bluewater Grill serves 95 covers for dinner and 40 covers for a separate lunch service on the same day, with dinner sales of $4,750 and lunch sales of $800. A manager wants the average check for dinner service only.

options.A: $41.11 as the average check for dinner service at the Bluewater Grill
options.B: $20.00 as the average check for dinner service
options.C: $58.42 as the average check for dinner service at the Grill that night
options.D: $50.00 as the average check for dinner service that night

explanation: Average check for dinner service is dinner sales divided by dinner covers, so $4,750 divided by 95 covers equals $50.00. Option A blends both services' sales and covers together, which conflates two separate services. Option B uses the lunch numbers, which gives the lunch average and not dinner's. Option C divides the combined sales of both services by just the dinner covers, overstating the rate by including lunch revenue dinner guests never generated.

performanceIndicator: Calculate gross operating profit per available room (GOPPAR)
question: The Hillcrest Hotel has 100 available rooms and reports a gross operating profit of $25,000 for the month. What is its GOPPAR?

options.A: $25,000.00, the profit without dividing by rooms
options.B: $100.00 GOPPAR figure
options.C: $2.50 GOPPAR per room
options.D: $250.00 GOPPAR per room

explanation: GOPPAR equals gross operating profit divided by available rooms, so $25,000 divided by 100 rooms equals $250.00. Reporting the $25,000 profit without dividing by the room count gives total profit, not a per-room figure, and $100.00 and $2.50 do not match the numbers given in the stem.

performanceIndicator: Calculate gross operating profit per available room (GOPPAR)
question: The Fairview Grand has 150 available rooms and reports total revenue of $450,000 for the quarter, with departmental and undistributed operating expenses of $270,000 for the same period. The general manager wants GOPPAR for the quarter.

options.A: $1,200.00, subtracting expenses from revenue and dividing by 150 rooms
options.B: $3,000.00, dividing total revenue alone by the available rooms
options.C: $450,000.00, the total revenue reported without any adjustment
options.D: $1,800.00, dividing total expenses alone by the available rooms

explanation: GOPPAR is gross operating profit, revenue minus operating expenses, divided by available rooms, so ($450,000 minus $270,000) divided by 150 equals $1,200.00. Dividing total revenue alone by the rooms ignores that expenses were reported at all. Reporting the total revenue undivided is not a per-room figure. Dividing the expenses alone by the rooms produces a cost figure, not a profit figure.

performanceIndicator: Calculate inventory turnover for food and beverage
question: A hotel restaurant's food cost of goods sold for the month is $48,000, and its average food inventory value is $8,000. What is the inventory turnover rate?

options.A: 8.00 inventory turnover
options.B: $8,000.00 inventory turnover at the hotel restaurant
options.C: 6.00 inventory turnover for the month
options.D: 0.17 inventory turnover for the month at the restaurant

explanation: Inventory turnover equals cost of goods sold divided by average inventory, so $48,000 divided by $8,000 equals 6.00 turns. Option D inverts the fraction, which gives the reciprocal and not the turnover rate. Option B restates the inventory value as a dollar figure rather than a rate. Option A does not match either number given.

performanceIndicator: Calculate inventory turnover for food and beverage
question: The Lakeshore Bistro's beginning food inventory was $6,000 and its ending food inventory was $10,000 for the month, during which the kitchen used $64,000 of food (cost of goods sold). The chef wants the inventory turnover rate using average inventory.

options.A: 6.4 inventory turns for the month
options.B: 10.67 inventory turns at the Lakeshore Bistro
options.C: 8.0 inventory turns
options.D: 0.125 inventory turns for the month at the Lakeshore Bistro

explanation: Inventory turnover uses average inventory, the beginning and ending values averaged together, so $64,000 divided by (($6,000 plus $10,000) divided by 2) equals 8.0 turns. Option A uses the ending inventory of $10,000 by itself, and option B uses the beginning inventory of $6,000 by itself; both skip the averaging step the formula requires. Option D inverts the fraction, which gives the reciprocal and not the turnover rate.

question: The Copper Kettle Cafe spends $4,500 on labor in a week when it records $18,000 in total sales. What is the labor-cost percentage?

options.A: 18% labor cost for the week
options.B: $4,500.00 labor cost at the Copper Kettle Cafe
options.C: 25% labor cost for the week at the Copper Kettle Cafe
options.D: 40% labor cost

explanation: Labor-cost percentage is wages divided by total weekly sales: $4,500 ÷ $18,000 = 25%, so option C is correct. Option A divides the wages by an incorrect sales figure of $25,000 ($4,500 ÷ $25,000 = 18%). Option D divides the wages by profit rather than by sales revenue. Option B restates the raw dollar wage instead of computing a rate.

question: The Riverside Tavern pays $6,200 in hourly wages and an additional $1,300 in payroll taxes and benefits for a week in which total sales reach $30,000. The owner wants labor cost as a percentage of sales, including taxes and benefits.

options.A: 20.7% of sales as labor cost for the week
options.B: 4.3% of sales as labor cost at the Riverside Tavern this week
options.C: 400.0% of sales as labor cost
options.D: 25.0% of sales as labor cost for the tavern's week

explanation: Labor-cost percentage should include every labor-related expense, so the $6,200 in wages plus $1,300 in taxes and benefits, divided by $30,000 in sales, equals 25.0%. Option A uses the hourly wages by themselves in the numerator, giving 20.7%, and option B uses the taxes and benefits by themselves, giving 4.3%; both leave out part of the labor cost. Option C divides total sales by total labor cost, which inverts the fraction and produces a meaningless 400.0%.

question: The Pinegrove Inn has 80 available rooms and sells 60 of them on a given night. What is the occupancy percentage?

options.A: 60% occupancy at the Pinegrove Inn that night
options.B: 80% occupancy for the night
options.C: 75% occupancy at the inn that night
options.D: 133% occupancy

explanation: Occupancy percentage is rooms sold divided by rooms available: 60 ÷ 80 = 75%, so option C is correct. Option A treats the raw count of rooms sold as if it were already the rate. Option B does the same with the available-room count. Option D inverts the formula, computing 80 ÷ 60 in place of 60 ÷ 80.

question: The Maple Court Hotel has 120 available rooms. On a night when 6 rooms were out of service for renovation, the hotel sold 91 of the rooms that were available for sale. The manager wants occupancy calculated against the rooms actually available for sale, not the full room count.

options.A: 75.8%, dividing rooms sold by the full 120-room count
options.B: 79.8%, dividing rooms sold by the 114 rooms available for sale
options.C: 125.3%, dividing the 114 available rooms by the 91 rooms sold
options.D: 85.1%, counting the 6 out-of-service rooms as sold along with the 91 sold rooms

explanation: Occupancy should be measured against rooms actually available for sale, so 91 rooms sold divided by 114 available rooms equals 79.8%. Dividing by the full 120-room count includes rooms that were never available for sale that night, understating the rate to 75.8%. Inverting the fraction gives an impossible value over 100%. Counting the 6 out-of-service rooms as sold overstates how many rooms actually generated revenue.

performanceIndicator: Calculate par stock and quantity to order
question: A bar's par stock for a liquor item is 24 bottles, and 9 bottles remain on the shelf at the start of the week. How many bottles should be ordered to bring stock back to par?

options.A: 15 bottles, par of 24 minus the 9 on hand already
options.B: 24 bottles, the full par stock amount
options.C: 9 bottles, the amount currently on hand
options.D: 33 bottles, par stock plus the amount on hand

explanation: The order quantity to reach par is the par stock minus what is already on hand, so 24 minus 9 equals 15 bottles. Ordering the full par amount of 24 ignores the 9 bottles already in stock, ordering just the 9 on hand does not restock anything, and adding the two figures together overshoots par instead of reaching it.

performanceIndicator: Calculate par stock and quantity to order
question: A hotel kitchen sets par stock for canned tomatoes at 60 cases. At Monday's inventory count, 22 cases remain on the shelf, and the chef also knows 8 cases are already on order from last week's delivery that has not yet arrived. How many cases should this week's order be to reach par without over-ordering?

options.A: 38 cases of canned tomatoes to order this week
options.B: 60 cases to order this week
options.C: 22 cases to order for the kitchen this week
options.D: 30 cases of canned tomatoes to order

explanation: The correct order accounts for everything already available, so par minus on-hand stock minus stock already on order, 60 minus 22 minus 8, equals 30 cases. Option A subtracts the on-shelf cases and skips the 8 already on order, which would create an over-order once that delivery arrives. Option B orders the whole par amount without subtracting anything. Option C reports the count already on the shelf rather than the quantity still needed.

performanceIndicator: Calculate recipe yield and number of portions
question: A soup recipe yields 8 quarts and each portion served is 1 cup (there are 4 cups in a quart). How many portions does the recipe yield?

options.A: 8 portions, one per quart produced
options.B: 4 portions, one per cup measurement
options.C: 32 portions, converting 8 quarts to cups, 4 per quart
options.D: 12 portions, quarts plus cups added together

explanation: Total portions equal total volume converted to the portion unit, so 8 quarts times 4 cups per quart equals 32 one-cup portions. Treating the quart count or the cup measurement alone as the portion count skips the conversion, and adding the two unlike numbers together has no basis in the recipe math.

performanceIndicator: Calculate recipe yield and number of portions
question: A caterer needs to scale a chili recipe that yields 5 quarts and 20 portions at its original size to instead serve 150 people at the same portion size, while also confirming how many quarts of chili that will require.

options.A: 150 quarts of chili for the caterer's 150 guests this weekend
options.B: 37.5 portions of chili for the caterer's guest count
options.C: 37.5 quarts of chili at the original portion size
options.D: 20 quarts of chili for the caterer's scaled recipe

explanation: The original recipe's ratio is 5 quarts for 20 portions, or 0.25 quart per portion; scaling to 150 portions at that same ratio requires 150 times 0.25, or 37.5 quarts. Reusing the 37.5 figure as a portion count instead of a quart count mislabels the correct number. Scaling the 20-portion figure by the 7.5x growth factor, rather than scaling the 5-quart yield by it, produces an unrelated total of 150. Using the original 20-quart figure without any scaling ignores that the caterer needs to serve far more than the original recipe's size.

question: The Northgate Hotel has 100 available rooms and generates $8,500 in room revenue over one night. What is its RevPAR?

options.A: $8,500.00 RevPAR at the Northgate Hotel
options.B: $85.00 RevPAR for the night at the Northgate Hotel
options.C: $100.00 RevPAR
options.D: $8.50 RevPAR for the night

explanation: RevPAR equals total room revenue divided by available rooms, so $8,500 divided by 100 rooms equals $85.00. Option A reports the revenue figure without dividing by the room count, which gives total revenue and not RevPAR. Options C and D do not match the numbers given.

question: The Coastal Palms Resort has 180 available rooms. Over a slow week, the resort generates $63,000 in room revenue, but 20 of the available rooms were closed for renovation and could not be sold. The controller wants RevPAR calculated against the rooms that were actually available for sale.

options.A: $350.00 RevPAR for the week
options.B: $3,150.00 RevPAR at Coastal Palms Resort
options.C: $63,000.00 RevPAR for the week at Coastal Palms Resort
options.D: $393.75 RevPAR

explanation: RevPAR should be measured against rooms actually available for sale, so $63,000 divided by the 160 available rooms (180 minus the 20 closed for renovation) equals $393.75. Option A divides by the whole 180-room count, which includes rooms that could not be sold that week and understates the rate. Option B divides by just the 20 closed rooms, confusing the excluded rooms with the denominator. Option C reports the $63,000 total without dividing by any room count, so it is not a rate at all.

performanceIndicator: Calculate table turnover rate and seats occupied
question: A dining room has 40 seats and serves 100 guests over the course of a dinner service. What is the table turnover rate for the evening?

options.A: 2.5 turns in the dining room
options.B: 40.0 turns in the dining room for the evening
options.C: 0.4 turns for the evening
options.D: 100.0 turns in the dining room

explanation: Table turnover rate equals guests served divided by seats available, so 100 guests divided by 40 seats equals 2.5 turns. Options B and D use the seat count or the guest count directly as the rate, which skips the division, and option C divides seats by guests served, inverting the fraction entirely.

performanceIndicator: Calculate table turnover rate and seats occupied
question: A restaurant's dining room has 50 seats. During a four-hour dinner service, the host seats 175 guests total, but the manager also learns that 15 of those guests were moved to overflow seating in the bar area rather than the dining room's 50 seats. The manager wants the table turnover rate for the dining room alone.

options.A: 3.5 turns for the dining room during dinner service at the restaurant
options.B: 0.3 turns for the dining room
options.C: 3.2 turns for the dining room at the restaurant
options.D: 3.8 turns for the dining room during dinner service

explanation: The turnover rate should use only the guests actually seated in the dining room, so 160 guests (175 total minus the 15 moved to overflow) divided by the 50 seats equals 3.2 turns. Option A divides all 175 guests, including the ones seated elsewhere, by the 50 seats, which overstates the rate. Option D double-counts the 15 overflow guests before dividing, producing an inflated rate. Option B divides the seats by the guests, inverting the fraction entirely.

question: A hotel's front office and housekeeping departments frequently miscommunicate about which rooms are ready for early check-in. What should the front office manager do to coordinate this activity with housekeeping going forward?

options.A: Have the front desk guess which rooms are ready
options.B: Wait until housekeeping submits its shift paperwork
options.C: Ask each guest to check their own room's status
options.D: Set up a shared real-time room-status system

explanation: Coordinating this activity well means giving both departments a shared, real-time way to see room status, rather than relying on guesswork, end-of-shift paperwork, or asking guests directly. Guessing which rooms are ready risks moving a guest into an unready room, waiting for shift paperwork delays the information by hours, and asking guests to check their own room status pushes hotel work onto the guest.

question: During a banquet setup, one server finishes assigned tables early while a teammate is still behind on table settings elsewhere in the room. What should the first server do?

options.A: Take an unscheduled break until service begins
options.B: Wait for a manager to issue a new written assignment
options.C: Keep resetting tables that are already finished
options.D: Help the teammate finish the remaining tables

explanation: Coordinating work with teammates means stepping in where the team's workload is unbalanced, so helping the teammate finish the remaining tables gets the room ready fastest. Taking an unscheduled break or re-resetting tables that are already finished wastes the extra capacity, and waiting for a new written assignment adds delay when the need is already obvious.

question: A kitchen line cook notices that the prep cook next to their station has fallen behind chopping vegetables, threatening to delay the dinner service. What is the best way for the line cook to coordinate with this team member?

options.A: Offer to help chop vegetables until caught up
options.B: Report the delay and keep working on unrelated tasks
options.C: Start plating dishes that are not yet ready
options.D: Ignore the delay; vegetables aren't this job

explanation: Coordinating work with a struggling teammate means pitching in directly, so offering to help chop vegetables gets dinner service back on schedule fastest. Reporting the delay and continuing on unrelated tasks wastes time that could go toward helping, plating dishes that are not ready creates new problems, and treating the delay as someone else's job ignores that the whole line depends on it.

question: Which regulation requires hotels to keep emergency exit routes clear and clearly marked with illuminated signage at all times?

options.A: The Fair Labor Standards Act, governing wages
options.B: The Americans with Disabilities Act, on access
options.C: State food safety code, covering sanitation
options.D: Fire and life-safety codes governing emergency egress

explanation: Fire and life-safety codes govern emergency egress requirements such as clear, illuminated exit routes, so fire and life-safety codes governing emergency egress is correct. The Fair Labor Standards Act, governing wages, addresses pay and work hours, not building safety; the Americans with Disabilities Act, on access addresses accessibility, not exit signage; and state food safety code, covering sanitation governs food handling, not emergency egress.

question: Which regulation requires housekeeping staff to wear gloves and follow specific handling procedures when they find a used needle or other sharp object in a guest room?

options.A: State liquor licensing law
options.B: General building maintenance codes for the property
options.C: OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard
options.D: The Fair Credit Reporting Act

explanation: OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard requires specific handling procedures, including gloves, whenever staff may contact blood or other potentially infectious materials such as a used needle. State liquor licensing law governs alcohol service, the Fair Credit Reporting Act governs background checks, and general building maintenance codes cover the physical structure, none of which addresses handling a biohazard.

question: Which technology allows a hotel's front desk to see, in real time, which rooms have been cleaned and inspected by housekeeping?

options.A: A point-of-sale system
options.B: A general email list shared by every department
options.C: A revenue management system
options.D: A housekeeping room-status system

explanation: A housekeeping room-status system updates room status in real time so the front desk always sees which rooms are clean and inspected. A point-of-sale system tracks purchases, a revenue management system sets pricing, and a general email list is not built for real-time status updates.

question: Which technology issues and deactivates a hotel guest's electronic room key and logs every time the door is opened?

options.A: A property system handling billing and reservations
options.B: A point-of-sale system
options.C: An electronic door-lock and keycard system
options.D: A revenue management system

explanation: An electronic door-lock and keycard system issues and deactivates room keys and logs every door access, which is exactly the function described. A point-of-sale system processes purchases, a revenue management system sets room pricing, and a property management system handles billing and reservations rather than door access specifically.

question: A hotel's front desk manager notices that guests are waiting several minutes at checkout because staff must manually calculate incidentals like minibar charges and parking fees before printing a folio. Which technology change would most directly reduce that wait?

options.A: Add more printers at the front desk
options.B: Train staff to mentally calculate every incidental charge before printing each folio
options.C: Integrate the point-of-sale and minibar systems with the PMS
options.D: Install a self-service kiosk in the lobby

explanation: The wait is caused by manual calculation at checkout, so integrating the point-of-sale and minibar systems with the property management system lets incidental charges post automatically and print instantly, which directly removes the manual step. Training staff to calculate charges mentally still requires manual work and is slower and more error-prone than automation. Adding more printers does not speed up the calculation that happens before printing. A self-service kiosk moves the task to the guest but does not fix the underlying manual calculation.

question: Before starting to plan a hotel's annual holiday open house, what should the event coordinator define first?

options.A: The exact seating chart for guests
options.B: The event's overall goal and success criteria
options.C: The color scheme for table linens
options.D: The playlist of background music

explanation: A project plan should start with the goal and how success will be measured, since every later decision, from seating to music, should serve that goal. Seating charts, linen colors, and music playlists are all details that come later in the planning process, not the starting point.

question: After setting the goal for a hotel's charity gala, what should the event coordinator create next to organize who does what and by when?

options.A: A task list with owners and deadlines
options.B: A guest seating chart
options.C: A dessert menu for the event
options.D: A detailed budget spreadsheet for every vendor

explanation: After the goal is set, a task list assigning owners and deadlines is what actually organizes who does what and by when. A seating chart and a dessert menu are individual event details, not planning tools, and a budget spreadsheet tracks costs rather than task ownership and timing.

question: A hotel is planning a three-day conference for 400 attendees. The event coordinator has set the goal and built a task list, but two department heads say they do not know which tasks depend on others being finished first, and deadlines keep slipping as a result. What should the coordinator add to the plan to fix this?

options.A: A longer task list with more individual line items
options.B: A bigger budget to cover potential delays
options.C: A larger planning committee with representatives from every department attending
options.D: Task dependencies showing what must finish before what

explanation: Slipping deadlines caused by unclear task order call for dependencies, a sequence showing which tasks must finish before others can start, not just more tasks or people. Adding more line items to the task list does not show the order those items must happen in. A bigger budget addresses cost, not sequencing. A larger planning committee adds more people to coordinate without solving the missing dependency information itself.

question: A purchasing manager is choosing between two food suppliers who offer the same price and quality. One supplier has been cited for underpaying workers; the other has a clean labor record. Which choice reflects ethical purchasing?

options.A: Choose the cited supplier since price is what matters
options.B: Choose whichever supplier delivers fastest
options.C: Split the order evenly between both suppliers
options.D: Choose the supplier with the clean labor record

explanation: Ethical purchasing weighs a supplier's labor practices alongside price and quality, so with price and quality tied, choosing the supplier with a clean labor record is the ethical choice. Choosing the cited supplier ignores its labor violations, choosing by delivery speed ignores ethics entirely, and splitting the order evenly still funds the supplier with the labor violation.

question: A restaurant's produce supplier occasionally uses child labor at overseas farms, which the purchasing manager has just learned. What should the manager do?

options.A: Continue the contract since prices are low
options.B: Renegotiate only the delivery schedule
options.C: Stop sourcing from that supplier for an alternative
options.D: Ask the supplier to lower prices further

explanation: Discovering child labor in the supply chain calls for cutting ties with that supplier and sourcing from an ethical alternative, since continuing the relationship funds the practice. Continuing the contract for its price, renegotiating only the delivery schedule, or asking for a further discount all keep the unethical supplier in place.

question: A hotel's purchasing manager finds that the lowest-priced linen supplier meets every quality standard but is significantly cheaper than competitors specifically because it pays workers below the legal minimum wage in its home country, which the manager confirms through an independent audit report.

options.A: Reject the supplier despite the price advantage and document the findings
options.B: Accept the supplier since the price advantage benefits the budget
options.C: Negotiate a lower price still, since the supplier accepts thin margins
options.D: Continue purchasing from the supplier quietly while searching for a replacement

explanation: Confirmed below-minimum-wage practices call for cutting ties immediately and documenting the audit findings, not continuing the relationship in any form. Accepting the supplier for the price advantage or negotiating an even lower price both keep funding the violation. Continuing to purchase quietly while searching for a replacement still keeps money flowing to the supplier during that search, which does not stop the harm.

question: A front desk agent notices the night auditor has been rounding up nightly parking fees and pocketing the difference in cash. What is the most ethical response for the front desk agent?

options.A: Personally confront the auditor and demand repayment
options.B: Say nothing since it isn't this agent's job
options.C: Tell a manager through the proper channel
options.D: Wait to see if it happens again before acting

explanation: The ethical response to suspected theft is to report it to a manager through the proper channel, not to handle it personally or ignore it. Confronting the auditor directly risks a dangerous or compromised confrontation without authority to investigate. Staying silent lets the theft continue, and waiting to see if it happens again delays a report that should happen now.

question: A restaurant server notices a coworker charging regular customers full price but comping drinks for personal friends without manager approval. What should the server do?

options.A: Start comping drinks for friends too
options.B: Say nothing to avoid a conflict
options.C: Confront the coworker during a busy dinner shift
options.D: Report the unauthorized comps to a manager

explanation: Unauthorized comps are a form of theft from the business, so the ethical response is to report them to a manager who can address it properly. Comping drinks for friends too would repeat the same unethical behavior, staying silent lets it continue, and confronting the coworker directly during a busy shift risks a public conflict without the authority to resolve it.

question: After a hotel's staff appreciation event ends, what is the best source of data for judging whether the event met its planning goals?

options.A: Informal comments gathered from a handful of staff
options.B: The total amount spent on decorations
options.C: Goals measured against attendance and feedback
options.D: The number of photos taken during the event

explanation: Evaluating project results means measuring the pre-event goals against real post-event data like attendance and feedback, which directly shows whether the goals were met. Informal comments from a handful of staff are not representative, and decoration spending or the number of photos taken measure inputs and mementos, not whether the goals were achieved.

question: A hotel's community outreach event set two goals beforehand: raise $5,000 for a local charity and attract 200 attendees. The event raised $4,200 and drew 240 attendees. The events manager needs to evaluate the project's results for the year-end report.

options.A: Report partial success: attendance succeeded, fundraising fell short
options.B: Report full success since more attendees usually leads to future donations
options.C: Report failure since the fundraising goal was not fully met
options.D: Report success since more people attended than planned

explanation: Evaluating results against both original goals shows a mixed outcome: attendance exceeded its target of 200 at 240, but fundraising fell short of the $5,000 goal at $4,200, so the honest report is a partial success on both counts. Calling it a full success because higher attendance might help future donations goes beyond what this year's actual data shows. Calling it a failure ignores that the attendance goal was clearly met. Calling it a success based on attendance alone ignores the fundraising shortfall entirely.

question: A hotel's new employee onboarding program was redesigned six months ago. Which piece of evidence best shows whether the redesign actually succeeded?

options.A: New-hire retention data from before and after
options.B: The number of slides in the onboarding deck
options.C: A small handful of comments the HR director recalls
options.D: How much the redesign cost to develop

explanation: Evaluating whether the redesign succeeded requires real outcome data, so retention and performance figures collected before and after the change are the direct evidence of impact. A small handful of comments the HR director happens to recall is anecdotal and not representative, and the number of slides in the deck or the redesign's development cost describe the effort put in, not whether it worked.

question: A hotel launched a new mobile check-in feature six months ago with the stated goal of cutting average front-desk wait time by 30% without reducing guest satisfaction scores. Data now shows wait time dropped by 34% and satisfaction scores rose slightly. A regional manager wants a defensible evaluation of the project.

options.A: Inconclusive, since satisfaction scores can fluctuate for other reasons
options.B: Failure, since wait-time gains are usually offset by lower satisfaction
options.C: Success, since the wait-time goal was exceeded and satisfaction did not decline
options.D: Success, based only on how many guests downloaded the mobile app

explanation: Both stated goals were checked against real data: wait time dropped 34%, beating the 30% target, and satisfaction rose rather than declined, so the defensible evaluation is success on both measured goals. Calling it inconclusive dismisses the two goals the project explicitly set out to measure. Calling it a failure assumes a tradeoff that the data does not show here. Judging success by app downloads alone ignores the wait-time and satisfaction goals the project was actually measured against.

question: Which criterion is most relevant when formally evaluating a linen supplier's performance over the past quarter?

options.A: Whether the sales representative is easy to talk to
options.B: On-time delivery and defect rates this quarter
options.C: The size of the supplier's logo on invoices
options.D: How long the supplier has existed as a company

explanation: Vendor performance is evaluated on concrete, measurable factors like on-time delivery and defect rates, since those directly affect hotel operations. Whether a sales representative is pleasant on the phone, how large a logo appears on an invoice, or how long the company has existed say nothing about the actual quality of what the vendor delivers.

question: A purchasing manager tracks three linen suppliers over the same quarter using identical scorecards covering delivery timeliness, defect rate, and responsiveness to complaints. What is the main benefit of using identical scorecards across all three suppliers?

options.A: It guarantees the cheapest supplier wins
options.B: It eliminates reading any delivery paperwork
options.C: It shortens each vendor contract's length
options.D: It allows a fair comparison across all vendors

explanation: Using identical scorecards across all three suppliers allows a fair, apples-to-apples comparison of their actual performance on the same criteria. It does not guarantee the cheapest supplier wins, since price is only one possible factor on the scorecard; it does not eliminate the need to review delivery paperwork, which still documents timeliness; and it has no effect on how long any contract lasts.

question: After any workplace accident involving a guest or employee has been handled and immediate safety needs addressed, what must staff do next according to standard accident procedures?

options.A: Complete a written incident report while it's fresh
options.B: Wait a few days to see if anyone complains
options.C: Discuss the accident on social media
options.D: Delete the surveillance footage right away

explanation: Standard accident procedure requires documenting what happened in a written incident report as soon as possible, while details are accurate and available for insurance, legal, and safety-improvement purposes. Waiting to see if a complaint is filed delays necessary documentation, discussing the incident on social media is unprofessional and can create liability, and deleting surveillance footage is both unethical and likely illegal.

question: A line cook suffers a minor burn on a stovetop during dinner service. A coworker helps them run the burn under cool water and get first aid, and the kitchen keeps operating. Twenty minutes later, the shift supervisor still has not been told about the incident. What should happen next, according to standard accident procedure?

options.A: Nothing further, since the injury was already treated with first aid
options.B: The supervisor should be notified immediately and an incident report started
options.C: The cook should finish the shift first and mention it during the closing meeting
options.D: The coworker who provided first aid should decide whether it's worth reporting

explanation: Every workplace injury, even a minor one already treated with first aid, must be reported to a supervisor right away so an incident report can be started while details are fresh. Treating the burn without ever notifying a supervisor leaves no record of the incident. Waiting until a closing meeting to mention it delays reporting for hours and risks it being forgotten. Leaving the reporting decision to the coworker who gave first aid is not how the reporting responsibility works, since a supervisor needs to know promptly no matter how minor the injury seems.

performanceIndicator: Explain employee role in expense control
question: A banquet server notices that after each event, several unopened bottles of water are thrown away instead of being saved for the next event or donated. What is the server's role in expense control here?

options.A: Take the bottles home for personal use
options.B: Flag it to a supervisor and suggest saving stock
options.C: Continue disposing of the bottles exactly as trained
options.D: Quietly stop restocking water at future events

explanation: An employee's role in expense control includes speaking up when they see resources being wasted, so flagging the practice to a supervisor and suggesting the stock be saved or donated actually reduces waste. Continuing to dispose of the bottles exactly as trained lets the waste continue unquestioned. Taking bottles home for personal use is a form of theft, not expense control, and quietly stopping restocking on one's own could leave future events short of water without the decision ever being reviewed.

question: Which of the following is a FIXED operating cost for a hotel, one that does not change with occupancy?

options.A: Monthly property insurance premium
options.B: Guest room cleaning supplies
options.C: Cost of amenities restocked in each occupied room
options.D: Laundry expense for used linens

explanation: A fixed cost like the monthly property insurance premium stays the same no matter how many rooms are occupied. Cleaning supplies, restocked amenities, and linen laundering all rise and fall with occupancy, which makes them variable costs instead.

question: Which of the following is a VARIABLE operating cost for a hotel, one that rises and falls with occupancy?

options.A: Annual property tax bill
options.B: Manager's fixed monthly salary
options.C: Guest room amenities and toiletries
options.D: The hotel's annual elevator maintenance contract

explanation: Guest room amenities and toiletries are restocked per occupied room, so their cost rises and falls directly with occupancy, making them the variable cost among these options. The annual property tax bill, the manager's fixed salary, and the elevator maintenance contract are all paid on a set schedule no matter how many rooms sell, making them fixed costs instead.

question: A boutique hotel's monthly operating statement lists $12,000 in departmental payroll that scales with occupancy, $8,000 in property insurance and debt service that stays constant every month, and $3,000 in guest supplies that also scales with occupancy. The general manager wants total operating costs classified correctly to build next year's flexible budget.

options.A: $15,000 variable (payroll and supplies) and $8,000 fixed (insurance and debt service)
options.B: $8,000 variable and $15,000 fixed, reversing which costs scale with occupancy
options.C: All $23,000 treated as fixed since it appears on the same monthly statement
options.D: All $23,000 treated as variable since occupancy affects the whole hotel

explanation: Correct classification separates costs by behavior, not by which statement they appear on: payroll and guest supplies both scale with occupancy for $15,000 in variable costs, while insurance and debt service stay constant at $8,000 in fixed costs. Reversing which costs are labeled variable and fixed misclassifies both categories. Treating everything as fixed ignores that payroll and supplies clearly move with occupancy, and treating everything as variable ignores that insurance and debt service do not change from month to month.

question: At a full-service hotel, which set of tasks falls under daily operations?

options.A: Auditing the annual marketing budget
options.B: Housekeeping, front desk, and food service
options.C: Negotiating the property's insurance renewal terms
options.D: Designing next season's advertising campaign

explanation: Housekeeping, the front desk, and food service are the day-to-day activities that keep a hotel running for guests, which is what operations covers. The other three options are important business functions, but they involve finance, insurance, and marketing rather than daily guest-facing operations.

question: A hotel's general manager says operations is the 'engine' of the property. Which statement best explains why daily operations matter to a hotel's success?

options.A: Smooth operations shape the guest experience and build repeat business.
options.B: Operations mainly decide which media channels the marketing team uses each season.
options.C: Operations set the interest rate on the hotel's construction loan.
options.D: Operations decide which accounting method the hotel uses for taxes.

explanation: Because operations covers every guest-facing process, from check-in to housekeeping, its quality directly shapes how guests rate their stay and whether they return, which is why it drives repeat business and revenue. Option B confuses operations with the marketing department's channel selection, a separate function. Option C describes a finance decision made by ownership, not daily operations. Option D describes an accounting policy choice, which sits in the finance function rather than operations.

question: A hotel guest asks the front desk to confirm whether another named guest is currently checked in. What should the associate do?

options.A: Decline to confirm any guest's stay to others
options.B: Confirm only the guest's room number
options.C: Share the guest's room number and departure date
options.D: Ask a manager to page the other guest overhead

explanation: Hotel guests' stay and room details are confidential and cannot be shared with anyone but the guest, so the associate should decline the request. The other three options each disclose protected guest information to someone who is not the guest.

question: A housekeeper finds a guest's passport left on the nightstand while cleaning the room. What should the housekeeper do?

options.A: Photograph the passport for the hotel's files
options.B: Leave it in place and notify a supervisor right away
options.C: Give it to another guest staying nearby
options.D: Secure it and turn it in to management

explanation: Guest identification documents are confidential property and should be secured and handed to management so the guest can retrieve it safely. The other options either fail to protect the document or improperly involve people who have no right to it.

question: Which characteristic distinguishes a project from a hotel's routine daily operations?

options.A: It requires assembling a brand-new project team
options.B: It is temporary with one specific goal
options.C: It repeats on an identical daily schedule
options.D: It rarely involves more than one department

explanation: A project is a temporary effort with a defined, specific goal, unlike the repeating, ongoing nature of daily operations. The other options describe traits that are not what actually separates a project from routine operations.

question: A catering company is opening a new banquet hall next quarter. Which activity best reflects project management rather than routine daily operations?

options.A: Building a timeline of milestones for permits, staffing, and opening day
options.B: Scheduling the banquet hall's weekly linen laundering pickup
options.C: Restocking the walk-in cooler after each event
options.D: Processing this week's payroll for banquet staff

explanation: Opening a new banquet hall is a one-time effort with a defined goal and deadline, so building a milestone timeline for permits, staffing, and the opening date is project management. Option B, weekly linen pickup, is a recurring operational task, not a one-time project. Option C, restocking a cooler, is routine daily operations. Option D, processing payroll, is also a recurring operational task rather than a temporary project.

question: Which task is part of a hotel's purchasing function?

options.A: Interviewing candidates for the front desk
options.B: Comparing supplier quotes before ordering
options.C: Reviewing the hotel's quarterly financial statements
options.D: Scheduling housekeeping shifts for the weekend

explanation: Purchasing includes comparing quotes from different suppliers before committing to an order, which helps the hotel secure the best value. The other options belong to human resources, finance, and scheduling rather than purchasing.

question: A restaurant's purchasing manager is choosing between two produce suppliers who offer similar prices. Which factor should most influence the decision?

options.A: The suppliers' company logos and marketing materials
options.B: Whichever supplier the manager has personally known the longest
options.C: The suppliers' locations relative to headquarters
options.D: Each supplier's delivery reliability and freshness record

explanation: When prices are similar, purchasing decisions should weigh which supplier reliably delivers on time and provides consistently fresh product, since that protects the restaurant's menu quality. Option A, logos and marketing materials, has no bearing on supply reliability. Option B, personal familiarity, is not a sound business criterion and risks favoritism over performance. Option C, office location relative to headquarters, does not indicate delivery performance to the restaurant itself.

question: How can poor purchasing decisions reduce a kitchen's productivity?

options.A: By increasing the number of loyalty program members
options.B: By raising the hotel's overall room rates
options.C: By causing supply shortages that stop kitchen workflow
options.D: By changing the color scheme of staff uniforms

explanation: When purchasing fails to keep needed items in stock, kitchen staff must stop working and improvise, which slows output and hurts productivity. The other options describe changes unrelated to purchasing's effect on how efficiently the kitchen operates.

question: How does buying reliable, well-suited kitchen equipment affect staff productivity?

options.A: It has no effect on how fast staff work
options.B: It mainly affects the restaurant's parking layout
options.C: It lets staff finish work faster with fewer breakdowns
options.D: It increases output by reducing equipment delays

explanation: Reliable, well-suited equipment reduces breakdowns and downtime, which increases how much staff can produce in a shift. The other options either deny an effect that exists or describe something purchasing decisions about kitchen equipment do not influence.

question: A hotel's purchasing department switches to a cheaper glassware supplier whose products break twice as often as the previous brand. What is the most likely effect on housekeeping productivity?

options.A: Housekeeping staff will need less training on glassware handling
options.B: Housekeeping will spend less time restocking room minibars
options.C: Housekeeping will lose time cleaning up breakage and replacing stock
options.D: Housekeeping will work faster since the new glasses are lighter to handle

explanation: Glassware that breaks twice as often forces housekeeping to stop their cleaning routine to sweep up broken pieces and pull replacement stock, which slows down how many rooms they can turn each shift. Option A wrongly assumes more fragile glassware needs less training, when it actually needs more care. Option B confuses glassware breakage with an unrelated task, restocking minibars. Option D assumes cheaper glass is lighter and easier to handle, but a higher breakage rate means more caution and lost time, not speed.

question: Why should hotel staff use the peephole before opening a guest room door for a maintenance request?

options.A: To confirm who is on the other side before opening
options.B: To check the hallway carpet for stains
options.C: To see if the elevator is currently in use
options.D: To avoid letting in someone unauthorized

explanation: Checking the peephole confirms who is at the door so staff do not let in someone who has no legitimate reason to be there, which is a basic security precaution. The other options describe unrelated observations that have nothing to do with verifying identity before opening a guest room door.

question: A restaurant chain's kitchen manager checks in regularly with its produce supplier's warehouse team to keep incoming shipments flowing smoothly and avoid running short on ingredients. What best describes this practice?

options.A: Aligning delivery schedules with the supplier
options.B: A one-time bulk discount negotiation
options.C: The supplier's separate internal staffing policy
options.D: A change in the restaurant's menu pricing

explanation: Regularly coordinating with a supplier's team so shipments arrive on time and inventory stays steady is a direct form of supply-chain collaboration, which is what aligning delivery schedules with the supplier describes.

question: A hotel chain and its uniform supplier begin sharing real-time inventory data so the supplier can automatically ship replacement stock before the hotel runs out. What benefit does this best illustrate?

options.A: It lets the supplier set the hotel's uniform design standards
options.B: It shifts all uniform costs from the hotel to the supplier
options.C: It replaces the hotel's need for a purchasing department
options.D: It reduces stockouts by letting the supplier react to real-time demand

explanation: Sharing real-time inventory data lets the supplier see actual usage and ship replacement stock proactively, which reduces the chance of running out before a scheduled reorder. Option A confuses data sharing with design authority, which the hotel still controls. Option B is incorrect because data sharing does not change who pays for uniforms. Option C is wrong because purchasing still negotiates contracts and approves spending; collaboration streamlines timing, not the department's existence.

question: Before using a commercial dishwasher for the first time, a new steward should first do what?

options.A: Ask a coworker to guess the settings
options.B: Copy the settings used on an older dishwasher model
options.C: Turn the water temperature to its highest setting
options.D: Read and follow the posted operating instructions

explanation: Commercial equipment varies by model, so a new steward should read and follow the manufacturer's posted instructions before first use to operate it safely and correctly. The other options each skip the instructions in favor of guessing, copying an unrelated machine's settings, or an arbitrary setting change.

question: A banquet cook is about to operate a large mixer for the first time and notices the posted instructions warn against running it above speed 4 with the dough hook attached. The cook needs speed 6 to finish on time. What should the cook do?

options.A: Follow the posted limit and find another way to finish the batch on time
options.B: Run it at speed 6 briefly since the deadline matters more than the warning label
options.C: Ask a server to hold the bowl steady while running it at speed 6
options.D: Switch to a different attachment without checking its own speed limit

explanation: Posted equipment limits exist to prevent damage or injury, so the cook should respect the speed-4 limit with the dough hook and find another way to meet the deadline, such as adjusting the process or asking for help. Option B ignores a stated safety limit to save time, which risks damaging the mixer or causing injury. Option C does not address the actual restriction, which is about motor speed with that attachment, not bowl stability. Option D swaps attachments without verifying its limit, which could create the same problem with a different part.

question: What is the correct way to carry a chef's knife while walking through a busy kitchen?

options.A: Hold it above the head, away from others
options.B: Point the blade down along the side of the leg
options.C: Carry it on a tray, fully covered with a clean towel
options.D: Hold it out in front to warn others nearby

explanation: Carrying a knife with the blade pointed down along the leg keeps the sharp edge away from other people and reduces the chance of an accidental cut while walking through a busy kitchen. The other options each keep the blade exposed or aimed toward people rather than safely down and to the side.

question: At the end of a shift, why should a front-desk associate log out of the property management system before leaving the terminal?

options.A: To free up space on the hard drive
options.B: To stop others from using their login and access
options.C: To restart the printer queue
options.D: To adjust the desk's monitor brightness

explanation: Logging out prevents anyone else from acting under the associate's credentials, which protects guest data and system access after the associate leaves the terminal. The other options describe unrelated, minor IT tasks that logging out does not accomplish.

question: A hotel's back-of-house door is propped open with a trash can on a hot day. What security procedure does this violate?

options.A: The dress-code policy for kitchen staff
options.B: The daily food-temperature log requirement
options.C: The rule keeping exterior doors closed and locked
options.D: The schedule for weekly linen delivery

explanation: Propping open an exterior door defeats the purpose of keeping unauthorized people out of the building, which is exactly what the closed-and-locked-door procedure is meant to prevent. The other options describe unrelated hotel policies that a propped-open door does not affect.

question: A front-desk associate notices a stranger without a staff badge following an employee closely through a badge-access door into the back office. What is the correct security response?

options.A: Politely stop the stranger and verify their reason for being there
options.B: Assume the person is a new hire who forgot a badge
options.C: Let the situation go since the employee already opened the door for them
options.D: Report it only if something goes missing later

explanation: Someone entering a badge-access area without their own credentials, known as tailgating, is a security risk regardless of who let them in, so the associate should stop the person and verify why they are there. Option B assumes good intent without verification, which is exactly the gap tailgating exploits. Option C excuses the breach because an employee opened the door, but the employee's badge does not authorize a second, unbadged person to enter. Option D waits for a loss to occur instead of addressing the security gap immediately.

question: A banquet server smells gas near the kitchen's stove line during service. What should the server do first?

options.A: Alert a manager and move guests away from the area
options.B: Light a candle to check for the gas smell
options.C: Evacuate the area and notify emergency services
options.D: Open a kitchen window and keep serving

explanation: A suspected gas leak requires evacuating the area and notifying emergency services right away, since gas is a life-safety hazard that trained responders must handle. The other options either delay evacuation, introduce an open flame near a gas leak, or continue normal service instead of clearing the area.

question: Which practice helps a restaurant catch inconsistent portion sizes before dishes reach guests?

options.A: Interviewing guests after they finish their meal
options.B: Reviewing last month's sales report
options.C: Rotating servers between sections weekly
options.D: Weighing portions against a standard before plating

explanation: Checking portions against a set standard before they leave the kitchen catches inconsistent sizes before guests ever see them, which is a direct quality-control measure. The other options happen after the fact or address unrelated areas like sales and staffing, not portion consistency.

question: A hotel's laundry service has received several complaints about stained linens reaching guest rooms. Which quality-control measure would most directly address this problem?

options.A: Inspecting linens under bright light before folding and storage
options.B: Increasing the laundry detergent order by twenty percent
options.C: Bringing it up casually at the next staff meeting without any formal inspection
options.D: Switching to a new linen supplier immediately

explanation: A direct visual inspection step, such as checking linens under bright light before they are folded and stored, catches stains before they reach a guest room, which is a genuine quality-control measure. Option B assumes the detergent quantity is the cause without evidence and does not add any inspection step. Option C raises awareness but has no formal check built into the process, so stained linens could still slip through. Option D is an overreaction that does not address whether the current process could catch the problem through inspection.

question: A front-desk associate steps away from the terminal to help a guest at the bell stand. The screen still shows a guest's reservation and payment details. What should the associate do first?

options.A: Ask a colleague to watch the screen for a minute
options.B: Turn the monitor to face the lobby windows
options.C: Lock the screen before leaving the terminal
options.D: Minimize the reservation window only

explanation: Locking the screen before stepping away immediately protects the guest's reservation and payment details from anyone who walks up to the terminal. The other options leave the sensitive screen visible or accessible to whoever is nearby, which does not secure the data.

question: A resort's IT department wants to reduce the risk of a data breach involving guests' stored payment information. Which policy would most directly reduce that risk?

options.A: Requiring all staff to share one login for faster check-ins
options.B: Requiring unique logins and limits on who can view payment data
options.C: Printing daily reservation lists for the break room
options.D: Emailing the daily guest list to all department heads

explanation: Unique logins create accountability for who accessed what, and limiting who can view payment data reduces the number of people who could expose it, which directly lowers breach risk. Option A actually increases risk because a shared login makes it impossible to trace who accessed guest data. Option C puts guest information on paper in a shared, unsecured space. Option D distributes guest information broadly to staff who may not need it, widening exposure instead of limiting it.

question: Why does a restaurant label each food container with the date it was opened?

options.A: To match the container's color to the shelf
options.B: To track which supplier delivered the item
options.C: To identify which manager approved the delivery
options.D: To know when to use or discard the item

explanation: Dating a container lets kitchen staff quickly see how long food has been open so they know when it should be used or thrown out, which keeps inventory safe and fresh. The other options describe details a date label does not communicate, such as color coding, supplier tracking, or purchase approval.

question: A catering company's par-level sheet shows the walk-in cooler is 15 pounds under its usual stock of chicken breast three days before a large event. What is the best inventory action to take?

options.A: Wait until the morning of the event to check stock again
options.B: Substitute a different protein without checking the event contract
options.C: Note the shortage informally and bring it up at the next team meeting
options.D: Place a reorder now so stock arrives before the event

explanation: Catching a shortage three days out gives enough lead time to place a reorder and have stock delivered before service begins, avoiding the risk of running out of a contracted item during the event.

question: A hotel maintenance worker finishes mopping a hallway near a guest elevator. What should the worker do before leaving the area?

options.A: Move the bucket to a locked closet
options.B: Set out a wet-floor sign until the floor dries
options.C: Ask the front desk to close the guest elevator
options.D: Prop a nearby door open so the floor airs out faster

explanation: A wet-floor sign warns guests and staff of the hazard until the floor is dry, which is the standard way to keep the area safe in the meantime. The other options either fail to warn anyone of the hazard or take an unnecessary and less effective step instead of posting a warning sign.

question: A hotel storage room has cleaning chemicals stacked in front of the fire exit. Which is the most serious safety issue this creates?

options.A: It makes weekly restocking take longer than usual
options.B: It blocks a required emergency exit path
options.C: It makes the room smell like cleaning chemicals
options.D: It uses extra shelf space in the closet

explanation: Stacking chemicals in front of a fire exit blocks a path required for emergency evacuation, which is a serious life-safety hazard regardless of how neatly the chemicals are stored. The other options describe minor inconveniences or non-hazard side effects that are not the actual safety issue the situation creates.

question: A hotel maintenance supervisor notices that several extension cords are being run across a busy kitchen walkway to power holiday decorations. What is the best long-term solution?

options.A: Tape the cords flatter against the floor so they lie lower
options.B: Reroute power through a nearby outlet, off the walkway
options.C: Post a sign warning staff to step over the cords carefully
options.D: Ask kitchen staff to remember the cords' location and walk around them

explanation: The best long-term fix removes the hazard entirely by rerouting power through an outlet near the decorations so no cord crosses the walkway at all. Option A reduces the trip risk slightly but still leaves a cord across a busy walkway. Option C relies on a warning sign rather than removing the hazard, so a distracted or new employee can still trip. Option D depends on every staff member's memory during a busy holiday season, which is not a reliable long-term fix.

question: A hotel is collecting bids from three landscaping companies for a new courtyard contract. What should the hotel do to keep the bid process fair?

options.A: Tell each bidder the lowest current bid so far
options.B: Award the contract to whichever company bids first
options.C: Give every bidder the same project specifications
options.D: Let a favored vendor see rivals' bids before revising

explanation: Giving every bidder identical project specifications ensures each company prices the same scope of work, which keeps the comparison and the process fair. The other options each give one bidder an unfair advantage or skip comparing bids on their merits altogether.

question: After receiving three sealed bids for a linen contract, what should a hotel purchasing manager do before opening any of them?

options.A: Wait until the submission deadline has fully passed
options.B: Open the bid from the largest company first
options.C: Call each bidder to ask about their price
options.D: Share the specifications with a new vendor

explanation: Waiting until the submission deadline has fully passed ensures every bidder had the same amount of time to submit, which keeps the process fair before any bids are opened. The other options open bids selectively, contact one bidder outside the process, or bring in a vendor who did not submit within the same timeline.

question: A hotel's purchasing manager receives a bid from a company owned by her cousin, along with two other bids for the same painting contract. What is the correct way to manage this?

options.A: Disclose the relationship in writing, then evaluate bids alongside a second reviewer
options.B: Disclose the relationship and let someone else evaluate the bids
options.C: Award the contract to her cousin's company since prices were similar
options.D: Keep the relationship private to avoid awkwardness

explanation: The correct response to a conflict of interest is full disclosure followed by recusal, letting someone without a personal stake evaluate the bids so the decision is unbiased. Option A discloses the relationship but still keeps the manager involved in evaluating, which does not remove the conflict just because a second reviewer is present. Option C lets the relationship influence the outcome instead of managing it. Option D hides a conflict of interest, which is the opposite of proper bid-process management.

question: A restaurant manager delegates weekly inventory counts to a shift lead. What is the best way to monitor that the task is being completed correctly?

options.A: Periodically spot-check counts against the shelves
options.B: Assume the counts are accurate once submitted
options.C: Ask another employee to redo the count secretly
options.D: Wait for a customer complaint before checking

explanation: Periodically spot-checking the shift lead's counts against the actual shelves lets the manager verify accuracy without redoing the whole task, which is effective monitoring of a delegated duty. The other options either assume accuracy without checking, undermine trust with a secret redo, or wait for a problem to surface instead of monitoring proactively.

question: A hotel housekeeping supervisor delegates room inspections to a senior room attendant. Which action shows the supervisor is still monitoring the delegated task?

options.A: Not mentioning the inspections again
options.B: Reviewing a sample of inspection reports each week
options.C: Stepping back from housekeeping decisions
options.D: Assuming attendants rarely make mistakes

explanation: Reviewing a sample of the attendant's inspection reports each week lets the supervisor confirm the delegated task is being done well without micromanaging it, which is active monitoring. The other options describe disengaging from the task entirely or assuming it is going fine without any actual check.

question: A catering director delegates menu-costing for a new event package to an assistant. Two weeks later, the assistant has not shared any progress. What is the best next step for the director?

options.A: Wait for the assistant to finish and simply hope the numbers turn out accurate
options.B: Check in with the assistant to review progress and offer help
options.C: Reassign the entire task to someone else immediately
options.D: Redo the costing herself without telling the assistant

explanation: When a delegated task has gone quiet for two weeks, checking in to see how it's progressing and offering support keeps the director informed while still letting the assistant own the work, which is effective monitoring. Option A abandons any oversight and hopes for the best, which defeats the purpose of monitoring a delegated task. Option C pulls the task away without first finding out what's happening, undermining the assistant unnecessarily. Option D quietly redoes the work instead of communicating, which does not build the assistant's ability to complete similar tasks in the future.

question: A front-desk associate has a long line of guests checking in and a ringing phone at the same time. What should the associate prioritize?

options.A: Answer the phone before helping any guest in line
options.B: Let the line grow while chatting with a coworker
options.C: Assist the guests already waiting in line immediately
options.D: Close the desk until the phone stops ringing

explanation: A phone call can usually be placed on hold or sent to voicemail, but guests already standing in line are waiting on service in person; assisting them immediately keeps check-in moving and protects the property's first impression.

question: A banquet server has three tasks before a wedding reception begins: setting tables, lighting candles, and restocking napkins. Lighting the candles takes the least time and can happen any time before guests arrive. Which task should the server do first?

options.A: Restock napkins after the tables are already set
options.B: Light the candles first since it's the fastest task
options.C: Set the tables first since it takes the longest
options.D: Skip napkins until after the reception starts

explanation: Starting with the task that takes the longest, setting the tables, makes the best use of the time before guests arrive, since the quick candle-lighting task can easily be fit in afterward. The other options either delay the longest task or skip a needed task rather than reordering it.

question: A hotel operations manager has four tasks due today: approving next week's staffing schedule, responding to a guest's written complaint, restocking the supply closet, and reviewing a vendor's routine invoice. Which should be handled first?

options.A: The guest's written complaint, since delayed responses hurt the stay
options.B: The staffing schedule, since it was due first thing this morning
options.C: The supply closet restocking, since the shelves look untidy
options.D: The vendor's routine invoice, since a late review delays payment by a day or two

explanation: A guest's written complaint should come first because an unanswered complaint keeps affecting that guest's experience the longer it waits, and guest satisfaction is the most time-sensitive of the four tasks. Option B is important but not as time-sensitive since the schedule was already due, not actively harming anyone by a short delay. Option C is a routine task with no real deadline pressure today. Option D, a routine invoice, can wait a day or two without meaningful consequence, unlike an unresolved guest complaint.

question: A restaurant's stock of olive oil will run out in two days, and the supplier needs three days' lead time to deliver. What should the kitchen manager do?

options.A: Wait until the oil runs out to order more
options.B: Order a different oil brand instead
options.C: Ask a nearby restaurant to lend some oil
options.D: Order today since lead time exceeds the days left

explanation: Since the supplier needs three days to deliver but only two days of oil remain, the kitchen manager must place the reorder today or the kitchen will run out before the new stock arrives. The other options either wait too long, switch products unnecessarily, or rely on an unreliable outside source instead of reordering on time.

question: A restaurant's usual paper towel supplier is out of stock for two weeks, and the restaurant has only a five-day supply on hand. What is the best action for the purchasing manager?

options.A: Place a temporary order with a backup supplier to bridge the gap
options.B: Wait the two weeks since switching suppliers takes extra approval time
options.C: Ration paper towels without telling any staff
options.D: Cancel all towel use until the supplier restocks

explanation: With only five days of supply against a two-week outage, ordering from a backup supplier bridges the gap so the restaurant does not run out before the usual supplier restocks. Option B accepts running out rather than solving the shortage, even though switching suppliers is a normal purchasing action, not an unusual one requiring extra delay. Option C hides a real shortage from staff instead of addressing it. Option D removes a basic supply entirely instead of finding an alternative source.

question: After the goals and budget for a new hotel loyalty-program launch are set, what is the next planning step?

options.A: Announce the launch date before assigning any tasks
options.B: Change the loyalty program's name
options.C: Cancel the budget approval meeting
options.D: Assign responsibilities and set milestone dates

explanation: Once goals and budget are set, the next planning step is to assign responsibilities and set milestone dates so the team knows who is doing what and by when.
